analysis.one_liner: Creates millions of public jobs, extends unemployment aid, and pays for it with taxes on millionaires, Wall Street trades, and oil companies.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 21 Democratic cosponsors in December 2011, never received a hearing or a vote in the Republican-led House and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill packages a long list of ideas to fight the unemployment crisis of 2011: direct federal money to hire teachers, police officers, firefighters, and health workers; to repair public schools; and to put hundreds of thousands of unemployed people to work on community projects. It extends emergency unemployment benefits and makes it illegal to refuse to hire someone just because they are unemployed. To pay for it, the bill raises tax rates on income above $1 million, applies Social Security taxes to income above $250,000, ends tax breaks for big oil companies, puts a small tax on Wall Street trades, and cuts the defense budget and the war in Afghanistan.
analysis.who_benefits: Unemployed workers and their families, through extended benefits, new public jobs, and a ban on job ads that exclude the unemployed. Public school students get safer, repaired schools. Communities get parks, weatherized homes, and rehabbed housing. Retirees and working families benefit from allowing Medicare to negotiate drug prices. Millions of wage earners gain from rules requiring companies to classify workers as employees with benefits rather than contractors.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes tens of billions of dollars a year to create specific numbers of jobs: 400,000 construction jobs and 250,000 maintenance jobs repairing public schools, 300,000 education jobs, 40,000 police officers, 12,000 firefighters, at least 40,000 health care workers, and 750,000 Community Corps jobs for the unemployed [S2][S3].
Extends emergency unemployment compensation until January 4, 2013, and lets states pay higher tiers of benefits [S2].
Makes it an unlawful employment practice for employers or job agencies to refuse to consider or advertise against hiring someone because they are unemployed [S2].

Raises top tax rates to as high as 49% on very high incomes, applies Social Security payroll tax to income above $250,000, ends multiple oil-company tax breaks, and puts a 0.03% tax on securities trades [S2].
Directs Medicare to negotiate prescription drug prices and creates a government-run public health insurance option on the exchanges [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Households with taxable income above $1 million, who would face new rates up to 49%; people with income above $250,000, who would pay Social Security tax on the excess; large oil companies, which would lose seven tax breaks; banks and brokers, who would pay a 0.03% tax on securities trades (part of which they typically pass on to investors, including retirement savers); profitable corporations holding cash, which face a temporary 40% surtax on retained earnings above their three-year average; and defense contractors, who lose the V-22 Osprey program and face a budget freeze at 2008 levels.
analysis.who_pays_short: Millionaires, oil companies, and Wall Street

drawbacks.text: The Wall Street trading tax would be partly passed through to ordinary investors, raising costs in mutual funds and 401(k) plans [S2].
The 40% surtax on corporate retained earnings penalizes companies for holding cash, which could discourage saving and investment even at firms not hoarding [S2].
The jobs spending is directly appropriated out of the Treasury before the new taxes take effect, so the bill could add to the deficit in the short run [S3].
Freezing the defense budget at 2008 levels and ending the V-22 Osprey program would cut jobs in defense-dependent communities [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefits are large and concrete: jobs, unemployment checks, school repairs, and lower drug prices for retirees. The main costs fall on very high earners, oil companies, banks, and defense firms, with some spillover to ordinary investors from the trading tax. The design is sprawling, a dozen bills stapled together with no chance of passage, and the near-term spending outruns the revenue it raises. But the core trade is straightforward: public spending on employment, paid for by taxing high income and financial transactions.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to 15 House committees on the day it was introduced, then scattered among subcommittees; it never got a hearing or a floor vote and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013 [S5][S1].

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva, co-chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, introduced the bill with Rep. Keith Ellison on December 13, 2011 [S3].
Twenty-one House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].
The Speaker assigned the bill to 15 committees at once, a pattern that signals a bill is not headed to the floor [S5].
After subcommittee referrals through February 2012, no further action was recorded, and the bill expired with the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Million-dollar earners, oil companies, banks, and defense contractors avoided the new taxes and cuts; no one received the bill's jobs or benefits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners, oil and drug companies

for.name: Rep. Raúl Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Act for the 99% and organized its package of job programs and tax increases.

for.name: 21 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party in the House, controlling the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a hearing or a floor vote in the 112th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; with Republicans holding the House majority, the bill received no hearing or vote [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill strips seven tax preferences, including percentage depletion and the domestic production deduction, and bars LIFO accounting for major integrated oil companies [S2].
A 0.03% excise tax on every securities trade would come out of trading revenue, part of it passed on to investors [S2].
Medicare would be required to negotiate Part D drug prices, threatening industry pricing power that today costs beneficiaries more [S2].
A government-run public insurance option on the exchanges would compete directly with private plans for customers [S2].
The bill freezes military spending at 2008 levels and terminates the V-22 Osprey program, cutting contracts; the same money would fund domestic jobs [S2].
Rules requiring accurate worker classification and misclassification penalties press firms to treat workers as employees with benefits, raising the firms' costs [S2].
School repair, community, and hiring grants are direct work for contractors and new public employees, with prevailing labor standards and Buy American rules attached [S3].
